text: The disappearance of it building implement is alleged to be the cause of a dispute between two employees, one an old man and the other little more than a youth. After high words had passed it is alleged that the young man who suspected the other of taking the tool, struck the old man with a knife in the abdomen. As a result of his injuries the man in question died at the Government Civil Hospital and the other is arraigned at the Criminal Sessions on a charge of murder.

label: text
text: He was represented this morning by Mr. H.S. Fitzroy and the Attorney General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., prosecuted.

label: text
text: The only alleged eye-witness is the man to whom belonged the tool which was the source of the trouble and on whose behalf the prisoner had taken up the cudgels. This man said that he saw prisoner strike the old man, with a knife and he (witness) then ran away. Later at a house at East Point he saw the prisoner who admitted that he had stabbed the man.

label: text
text:
This witness was cross-examined, minutes by Mr. Fitzroy. Asked to account for the fact that it was he (witness) and not the prisoner who stayed away from work for two days and seemed to have most apprehensions, whereas prisoner went on with his work the witness replied that he ran away and hid because he thought if the police could not get the prisoner they would come for him.
Witness maintained that he had heard the prisoner make the statement as to having stabbed the old man. This despite the fact that Mr. Fitzroy pointed out that another man who had heard the alleged confession stated in the witness box that he was the only person there at the time the confession was made.
Medical evidence of the terrible nature of the wounds from which the old man died was given and cross-examined by Mr. Fitzroy witnesses said that they did not think that the wound could have been self-inflicted through the old man falling on the weapon clenched in his own hand.

label: text
text: An Indian named Chanda Singh was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning to answer a charge under the passport regulations to which he pleaded guilty.

label: text
text:
Mr. T. H. King (Director of Criminal Intelligence) said that he would not press the charge, but he desired to see a conviction registered and a warning given to the man as His Worship thought fit. Under the regulations, Mr. King, said, it was necessary for people like the defendant to have a passport or certificate of identity before entering the Colony. Defendant had served as a ship's guard from October 1923 to September this year, and resigned shortly after he was brought up on a departmental charge for bringing a man into the Colony without any papers. It was therefore desirable to keep track of defendant's movements. The man had recently travelled to Shanghai and back without a permit.
His Worship told the defendant that he should be perfectly aware of the laws of the country. Under the offence, with which he was charged he was liable to a fine of $250, and six months' imprisonment. He would be let off lightly this time with a fine of $10, but a repetition of the offence would be met with heavy punishment.

text: It is proposed to hold a novices tournament open to all, on November 30 and December 1 and 7. The preliminary rounds will be fought on the first two days at Murray Barracks (by kind permission of the East Surrey Regiment) and the finals at the City Hall on December 7. The competition will be under Imperial Services Boxing Association Rules for competitions with any variations made by the Association's Boxing Committee.

label: text

label: text

text: Squadron Leader, Comingham and Flight-Lieutenants Bowley and Baggs who left Helouan at 7 a.m. on October 27 on three D.H. 9a machines on a flight to Nigeria and back, have arrived at Helouan on their return from Kano.

label: text
text: The Air Ministry had made arrangements for the dispatch this autumn from Cairo to Kano, in Nigeria, of a flight of three Service aircraft, from No. 47 Squadron of the Royal Air Force stationed at Heluan, Egypt. The flight was undertaken for the purpose of gaining experience, in long-distance flights over tropical countries where few facilities in the way of the ground organisation required by aircraft exist, and with the object of allowing Nigeria to see the capabilities of British aircraft. The route followed was through the Sudan, French Equatorial Africa, passing Lake Chad to Kanb, the capital of Nigeria. The place visited for refuelling, etc., were Aswam, in Egypt; Khartoum, El Obedi, and El Fasher, in the Sudan; Abecher and Fort Lamy, in French Equatorial Africa; and Maidugari and Kano, in Nigeria. The organisation of the flight was undertaken by Air Vice-Marshal Sir Oliver Swann, Air Officer Commanding, Middle East, Squadron Leader, A. Comingham in command of the flight.
